title: If it happens
description: Talk about what will happen, and what would happen.

explanation.summary: Spanish has a conditional that English does not: the word would in a sentence like I would go is a real verb form in Spanish, hablaría. It is used for what would happen, and it is the polite way to say what you think should happen.

sections.heading: The conditional
sections.body: The endings are -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. For -ar verbs they look like the imperfect of -er verbs: hablar, hablaría, hablarías, hablaría. For -er and -ir verbs they look the same: comer, comería; vivir, viviría. Ir is irregular: iría.

examples.en: I would go to your house.
I would live in the countryside.

sections.heading: If, then
sections.body: Spanish uses si for if and no then, but the word order changes: the conditional comes first and si comes after it. Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría. If you put si first, as in English, it is wrong.

examples.en: If I had time, I would travel.

examples.es: Si hace buen tiempo, iremos a la playa.
examples.en: If the weather is good, we will go to the beach.
If it does not rain, we will go out.

sections.heading: What you think should happen
sections.body: The conditional is also how you advise: deberías descansar. You should rest. Deberías comes from deber, which means to owe or must, so the idea is you owe yourself a rest.
